name: Eager vs Lazy Loading
overview: Pay at startup or at first use. Compare the bill for loading Spring beans and JPA associations, then decide what each use case needs.

sections.title: When Spring creates the bean
sections.content: Spring usually creates non-lazy singletons at startup. Lazy initialization can defer work, but an eager singleton that directly needs the bean may still trigger creation.

images.alt: When does Spring create a bean?
images.caption: Lazy creation can defer work. A dependency needed at startup can still be created early.

sections.title: When JPA fetches data
sections.content: Eager and lazy fetching control when related data becomes available. Inspect the SQL for excess data or an N+1 query pattern.

sections.title: Decide for the use case
sections.content: Create critical services early when startup validation matters. Fetch required associations inside the persistence context, using a query that suits the use case.

keyPoints: Choose when to initialize one costly bean and when to fetch one association. Say which delay you accept and how you'd measure it.

interviewQA.question: Can a lazy bean still start eagerly?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. An eager singleton may need it during startup.

interviewQA.question: Why might accessing a lazy association fail?
interviewQA.answer: An unloaded association may need an open persistence context to fetch its data.
